LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Quiz • Judicial review and constitutional supremacy
Explain why a constitutional organ described as the sole judge of an electoral contest may still be reviewed by the Supreme Court for jurisdictional error.

Answer: The organ's merits determination is exclusive, but it remains confined by the Constitution and is reviewable for grave abuse or jurisdictional excess.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution vests judicial power, including the duty to determine grave abuse of discretion. José A. Angara v. Electoral Commission, G.R. No. 45081, July 15, 1936, teaches that Judicial review enforces constitutional boundaries even when a constitutional organ is the sole judge within its assigned sphere.

Application: If an electoral tribunal refuses to hear a contest the Constitution places within its authority, or decides one outside it, judicial review corrects the boundary error without retrying ordinary factual merits.

Conclusion: The Supreme Court may review jurisdictional or grave-abuse questions despite the tribunal's sole-judge clause.

Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution vests judicial power, including the duty to determine grave abuse of discretion. Case authority: José A. Angara v. Electoral Commission, G.R. No. 45081, July 15, 1936.
Constitutional supremacy makes each branch supreme only within its assigned sphere; judicial review polices constitutional boundaries.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Quiz • Expanded judicial power
May the House avoid judicial review of its impeachment rules by invoking separation of powers?

Answer: No. Separation of powers protects legitimate legislative discretion but not grave abuse or violation of express constitutional restraints.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 1 and Article XI, Section 3 of the Constitution govern judicial review and impeachment. Ernesto B. Francisco, Jr. v. House of Representatives, G.R. Conclusion: The rule and proceeding are reviewable and invalid if they breach the one-year bar.

After the annual budget becomes law, legislators are authorized to select the local projects and beneficiaries that executive agencies must fund; is the arrangement valid?

Conclusion: The transfer is unconstitutional.

May minors bring an action to stop allegedly destructive logging that threatens resources they and future generations will need?

May government peace negotiators sign an agreement immediately creating an associative territorial entity with powers unavailable under the Constitution and existing autonomy statutes?

Conclusion: The agreement is invalid to the extent it exceeds present authority.

A government corporation conveys newly reclaimed submerged land directly to a private corporation without a presidential classification declaring it alienable; is the conveyance valid?

A child was born outside marriage to a Filipino father and an alien mother in 1968; does illegitimacy by itself prevent Philippine citizenship by blood?

Application: If reliable evidence proves the Filipino father's filiation, birth outside marriage alone does not defeat citizenship.

Conclusion: The child is Filipino by blood, subject to proof of filiation and the constitution in force at birth.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Midterm • Foreign passport after renunciation
A dual citizen signs the statutory personal renunciation required to run for mayor but uses a foreign passport twice before filing the certificate of candidacy; is the candidate qualified?

Answer: No. The passport use is a positive act representing foreign nationality and recants the required personal and sworn renunciation.

Legal Basis: Article IV, Section 5 and R.A. No. 9225, Section 5(2), govern dual-citizen candidacy. Casan Macode Maquiling v. Commission on Elections, Rommel Arnado y Cagoco, and Linog G. Balua, G.R. No. 195649, April 16, 2013, teaches that Use of a foreign passport after renunciation recants the oath of renunciation required of a dual citizen seeking elective office.

Application: Using the foreign passport after renunciation contradicts the representation that foreign citizenship was personally renounced.

Conclusion: The candidate is disqualified unless the controlling facts materially differ.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Midterm • Dual citizenship and dual allegiance
Distinguish dual citizenship from dual allegiance and state why the Constitution treats them differently.

Answer: Dual citizenship may arise involuntarily from different nationality laws, while dual allegiance is a conscious simultaneous loyalty to two states and is constitutionally inimical.

Legal Basis: Article IV, Section 5 addresses dual allegiance, while R.A. No. 9225 governs retention and reacquisition. Casan Macode Maquiling v. Application: A child who acquires two nationalities by descent has dual citizenship; an office seeker who deliberately continues exercising foreign political allegiance presents the different concern.

Conclusion: The law may accommodate dual citizenship while demanding acts that remove disqualifying dual allegiance.

Article IV, Section 5 addresses dual allegiance, while R.A. No. 9225 governs retention and reacquisition. Case authority: Casan Macode Maquiling v. Commission on Elections, Rommel Arnado y Cagoco, and Linog G. Balua, G.R. No. 195649, April 16, 2013.

Constitutional Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Midterm • Internal legislative rules
May a court nullify a statute solely because a chamber allegedly violated one of its waivable internal parliamentary rules during passage?

Answer: Ordinarily no. Courts do not enforce merely internal rules that a chamber may waive, unless the violation also breaches an express constitutional requirement or protected right.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Sections 16 and 26 distinguish internal procedural authority from mandatory constitutional lawmaking requirements. Joker P. Arroyo, Edcel C. Lagman, John Henry R. Osmeña, Wigberto E. Tañada, and Ronaldo B. Zamora v. Jose De Venecia, Raul Daza, Rodolfo Albano, the Executive Secretary, the Secretary of Finance, and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 127255, August 14, 1997, teaches that Courts generally will not invalidate a statute for an alleged violation of internal legislative rules unless a constitutional requirement is breached.

Application: If the alleged defect concerns only the sequence chosen under a chamber rule and the enrolled law satisfied constitutional readings and voting, invalidation is unwarranted.

Conclusion: The statute stands absent a constitutional violation or grave abuse affecting enforceable rights.

Article VI, Sections 16 and 26 distinguish internal procedural authority from mandatory constitutional lawmaking requirements. Case authority: Joker P. Arroyo, Edcel C. Lagman, John Henry R. Osmeña, Wigberto E. Tañada, and Ronaldo B. Zamora v. Jose De Venecia, Raul Daza, Rodolfo Albano, the Executive Secretary, the Secretary of Finance, and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 127255, August 14, 1997.
Separation of powers gives each chamber control of its proceedings, but constitutional commands remain judicially enforceable.

A litigant attacks a statute by presenting a legislator's affidavit that the chamber did not follow an internal amendment rule, although the enrolled bill is duly authenticated; should the affidavit prevail?

Legal Basis: Article VI, Sections 16(4) and 26 specify journal and lawmaking requirements. Joker P. Arroyo, Edcel C. Lagman, John Henry R. Osmeña, Wigberto E. Tañada, and Ronaldo B. Zamora v. No. 127255, August 14, 1997, teaches that Courts generally will not invalidate a statute for an alleged violation of internal legislative rules unless a constitutional requirement is breached.

Application: The affidavit concerns an internal amendment practice, not a missing constitutionally mandated recorded vote.

Conclusion: The challenge should fail.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Midterm • One-subject and title rule
A postal-service reform statute titled as such also withdraws government franking privileges; is that provision automatically void because the title does not mention franking?

Answer: No. The title need not be an index; a provision survives when it is germane to the single general subject expressed.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 26(1) requires one subject expressed in the title. Philippine Judges Association v. Pete Prado, G.R. No. 105371, November 11, 1993, teaches that A statute's title need not index every detail if the provision is germane, but irrational discrimination violates equal protection.

Application: Franking affects postal revenue and operations and is reasonably connected to postal-service reform.

Conclusion: The provision is not invalid on title grounds alone.
Article VI, Section 26(1) requires one subject expressed in the title. Case authority: Philippine Judges Association v. Pete Prado, G.R. No. 105371, November 11, 1993.
The rule prevents surprise and logrolling, not concise titles that fairly encompass related details.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Midterm • Question hour and legislative inquiry
Distinguish the congressional question hour from an inquiry in aid of legislation when a department secretary is summoned.

Answer: The question hour under Article VI, Section 22 concerns departmental matters and attendance of department heads depends on presidential consent; an inquiry under Section 21 supports legislation, follows published rules, and respects affected persons' rights.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Sections 21 and 22 separately govern the two mechanisms. Senate of the Philippines v. Eduardo R. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006, teaches that Executive privilege must be specifically invoked; department heads need presidential consent for a question-hour appearance, but inquiries in aid of legislation are separately governed.

Application: A hearing on a specific pending bill with duly published inquiry rules points to Section 21; general policy interpellation of a secretary points to Section 22.

Conclusion: The controlling safeguards depend on the proceeding's real purpose and design.
Article VI, Sections 21 and 22 separately govern the two mechanisms. Case authority: Senate of the Philippines v. Eduardo R. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006.
Congress cannot evade Section 22 by relabeling a question hour, and the Executive cannot use consent to defeat a genuine Section 21 inquiry.

A memorandum orders all executive officials to ignore every legislative summons because executive privilege might arise; is the blanket instruction valid?

Answer: No. Executive privilege must be specifically invoked by the President or proper authority and justified as to particular information; it is not a presumptive exemption from legislative process.

Legal Basis: Articles VI, Section 21 and VII, Section 1 support legislative inquiry and qualified executive confidentiality. Senate of the Philippines v. Eduardo R. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006, teaches that Executive privilege must be specifically invoked; department heads need presidential consent for a question-hour appearance, but inquiries in aid of legislation are separately governed.

Application: Because the memorandum supplies no question-specific basis and covers officials and topics indiscriminately, it exceeds the privilege.

Conclusion: The blanket instruction is invalid.

Articles VI, Section 21 and VII, Section 1 support legislative inquiry and qualified executive confidentiality. Case authority: Senate of the Philippines v. Eduardo R. Ermita, G.R. No. 169777, April 20, 2006.

A presidential adviser refuses to answer whether the President directed approval of a pending major contract, asserting confidential presidential communications; what must be shown?

Application: A direct presidential instruction on contract approval fits the presumptive core, but a properly supported compelling legislative need may still require disclosure.

Conclusion: The court must apply the qualified, communication-specific test.

Senate Committee on Accountability of Public Officers and Investigations, G.R. No. 180643, March 25, 2008.

A grave national-security crisis presents an urgent problem not expressly assigned by statute or constitutional text; may the President act solely because the action seems useful?

What must the President constitutionally establish before placing a region under martial law?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Final • Protection of judicial appropriations
May an item veto cancel a statutory adjustment in retired justices' benefits when the measure is not a separable appropriation item but a substantive condition implementing judicial fiscal autonomy?

Application: If the adjustment is an integral substantive directive rather than a discrete sum, cancellation exceeds item-veto authority.

Conclusion: The veto is invalid to that extent.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD301 • Final • Hierarchy of courts
A corporation files an original fact-heavy petition directly in the Supreme Court because the Court has concurrent jurisdiction; should direct resort be allowed?

Answer: Ordinarily no. Concurrent jurisdiction does not create an unrestricted choice of forum; the hierarchy of courts and need for fact-finding require filing in the proper lower court absent a recognized exceptional reason.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 5 defines Supreme Court jurisdiction, while procedural rules implement orderly review. GIOS-SAMAR, Inc. v. Department of Transportation and Communications, G.R. Conclusion: The petition should be dismissed without prejudice to proper filing.

A statute computes local-government shares only from national internal revenue taxes and excludes customs duties and other national taxes; is that limitation constitutional?

A people's initiative proposes replacing the presidential-bicameral system with a parliamentary-unicameral system; is this an amendment reachable by initiative?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Mala in se and mistake of fact
What is a mistake of fact, and when does it exempt an accused from criminal liability?

Answer: It is a misapprehension of fact that negates criminal intent when the act would have been lawful had the facts been as reasonably believed, the intention was lawful, and the actor was without fault or negligence.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 1 and 3 require dolo or culpa for felonies; mistake of fact is a jurisprudential application of the intent requirement. United States v. Ah Chong, G.R. No. L-5272, March 19, 1910, teaches that An honest mistake of fact may negate criminal intent when the act would have been lawful had the facts been as reasonably believed and the actor was without fault.

Application: A homeowner who reasonably mistakes a violent intruder for an attacker may lack dolo, while one who shoots without checking an obvious innocent target remains at fault.

Conclusion: A complete, non-negligent mistake of fact negates liability for the intentional felony.

Revised Penal Code Articles 1 and 3 require dolo or culpa for felonies; mistake of fact is a jurisprudential application of the intent requirement. Case authority: United States v. Ah Chong, G.R. No. L-5272, March 19, 1910.
The mistake must be honest and reasonable; it does not excuse negligence, bad faith, or liability for a mala prohibita offense whose statute dispenses with intent.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Error in personae
Distinguish error in personae from mistake of fact.

Answer: Error in personae occurs when the offender intends a criminal attack but mistakes the victim's identity, so criminal intent remains; mistake of fact is an honest, non-negligent factual error that would make the act lawful and may negate intent.

Application: Shooting B while intending to murder A is error in personae; striking a reasonably perceived unlawful aggressor who was actually innocent may be mistake of fact.

Conclusion: Error in personae ordinarily preserves liability; qualifying mistake of fact may exempt.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Impossible crime elements
Enumerate the elements of an impossible crime under the Revised Penal Code.

Answer: The offender must perform an act that would be an offense against persons or property; act with evil intent; face inherent impossibility of accomplishment or inadequate or ineffectual means; and commit no other violation of law.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 4(2), in relation to Article 59, defines and penalizes impossible crimes. Jacinto Intod v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103119, October 21, 1992, teaches that An impossible crime exists when the intended offense against persons or property is inherently impossible or accomplished with inadequate or ineffectual means, absent another violation.

Application: Shooting an empty bed while intending to kill its absent occupant may qualify if no property damage or other crime is committed.

Conclusion: All statutory elements, including absence of another violation, must concur.
Revised Penal Code Article 4(2), in relation to Article 59, defines and penalizes impossible crimes. Case authority: Jacinto Intod v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103119, October 21, 1992.
The provision punishes demonstrated criminal perversity while reserving impossible-crime treatment for conduct that produces no other offense.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Inherent impossibility
A gunman fires repeatedly into the victim's bedroom intending to kill her, but she is abroad and the bullets damage nothing; is attempted murder the proper charge?

Answer: No. Because the intended victim was physically absent and accomplishment was inherently impossible, the proper offense is an impossible crime, assuming no other violation was committed.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 4(2), 6, and 59 distinguish impossible crime from attempt. Jacinto Intod v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103119, October 21, 1992, teaches that An impossible crime exists when the intended offense against persons or property is inherently impossible or accomplished with inadequate or ineffectual means, absent another violation.

Application: The empty room made death impossible regardless of further acts, and the hypothetical excludes independent damage.

Conclusion: Liability is for an impossible crime, not attempted murder.
Revised Penal Code Articles 4(2), 6, and 59 distinguish impossible crime from attempt. Case authority: Jacinto Intod v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 103119, October 21, 1992.
Attempt presupposes that completion was possible but interrupted by a cause independent of the offender's will; factual impossibility present from the outset points to Article 4(2).
Jacinto Intod v. Court of Appeals
G.R. No. 103119, October 21, 1992; ponente: Davide, Jr., J.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Ineffectual means
A person, intending to kill, secretly mixes a harmless pinch of sugar into another's drink because he irrationally believes it is lethal poison; no other offense results. Is there criminal liability?

Answer: Yes, potentially for an impossible crime because the means employed were objectively inadequate or ineffectual despite evil intent.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 4(2) and 59 cover inherent impossibility and inadequate or ineffectual means. Jacinto Intod v. Court of Appeals, G.R. Application: Sugar cannot kill in the manner intended, yet the actor performed an overt act manifesting the criminal purpose and caused no other violation.

Conclusion: The facts satisfy impossible-crime treatment, subject to proof of intent.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Stages of theft
Is there a frustrated stage of theft under the Revised Penal Code?

Answer: No. Theft is consummated once the offender gains possession and control of the property with intent to gain, even if the offender cannot freely dispose of it.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 6 and 308 define stages generally and theft specifically. Rodolfo Valenzuela v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007, teaches that Theft is consummated upon unlawful taking with intent to gain; there is no frustrated stage of theft.

Application: A shoplifter who removes goods from the owner's control but is caught at the exit has consummated theft.

Conclusion: Liability is consummated theft, not frustrated theft.
Revised Penal Code Articles 6 and 308 define stages generally and theft specifically. Case authority: Rodolfo Valenzuela v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007.
Unlawful taking, not successful escape or disposal, completes theft; the statutory elements leave no intermediate frustrated stage.
Rodolfo Valenzuela v. People of the Philippines
G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007; ponente: Tinga, J.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Quiz • Consummation versus attempted theft
A would-be thief inserts a hand into an empty pocket intending to take a wallet but obtains nothing; distinguish the result from consummated theft.

Answer: There is no completed taking because no property passed into the offender's control; on the stated facts, the inherently impossible taking may constitute an impossible crime if Article 4(2)'s other elements are proved, while attempted theft applies if a wallet existed but an independent cause stopped the taking.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 4(2), 6, 51, and 308 supply the distinction. Rodolfo Valenzuela v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007, teaches that Theft is consummated upon unlawful taking with intent to gain; there is no frustrated stage of theft.

Application: The empty pocket makes taking that supposed wallet impossible, unlike interruption just before grasping an existing wallet.

Conclusion: The stated facts support impossible-crime treatment, not consummated theft; a factual change may instead support attempt.
Revised Penal Code Articles 4(2), 6, 51, and 308 supply the distinction. Case authority: Rodolfo Valenzuela v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007.
Consummated theft requires actual taking; attempt and impossible crime turn on whether an object existed and whether completion was possible.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Attempted rape and penetration
When is rape by penile penetration consummated rather than merely attempted?

Answer: It is consummated by the slightest penetration into the cleft of the labia majora; complete penetration, hymenal rupture, or ejaculation is unnecessary.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 6, 266-A, and 266-B, as amended, govern stages and rape. People of the Philippines v. Efren Agao y Añonuevo, G.R. No. 248049, October 4, 2022, teaches that For rape through penile penetration, consummation requires contact with the vulval cleft or cleft of the labia majora; mere surface contact outside that threshold may constitute attempt when Article 6 is otherwise satisfied.

Application: If the penis merely touches the outer surface before the attacker is stopped, the stage is attempted; any entry into the cleft consummates.

Conclusion: The physical finding of slightest labial-cleft penetration controls the stage.
Revised Penal Code Articles 6, 266-A, and 266-B, as amended, govern stages and rape. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Efren Agao y Añonuevo, G.R. No. 248049, October 4, 2022.
External contact without entry into the labial cleft may constitute attempt when overt acts directly commence rape and intervention prevents completion.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Spontaneous desistance
An assailant removes an adult victim's clothing and positions himself to rape her but voluntarily stops before any genital contact, without outside interruption; is he liable for attempted rape?

Answer: Not for attempted rape if the desistance was truly spontaneous before all acts of execution, because Article 6 excludes failure resulting from the actor's own spontaneous desistance; liability for independently completed acts remains.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 6 defines attempt and spontaneous desistance, while Articles 266-A and 266-B define rape. People of the Philippines v. Efren Agao y Añonuevo, G.R. No. 248049, October 4, 2022, teaches that For rape through penile penetration, consummation requires contact with the vulval cleft or cleft of the labia majora; mere surface contact outside that threshold may constitute attempt when Article 6 is otherwise satisfied.

Application: The facts attribute noncompletion solely to the offender's voluntary abandonment before penetration or direct genital contact.

Conclusion: Attempted rape does not attach, but acts such as coercion or physical injuries may be separately punishable.

Revised Penal Code Article 6 defines attempt and spontaneous desistance, while Articles 266-A and 266-B define rape. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Efren Agao y Añonuevo, G.R. No. 248049, October 4, 2022.
Desistance is a legal absolutory cause for the attempted felony, not erasure of other crimes already completed.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Battered woman syndrome
Does proof that an accused is a battered woman automatically establish complete self-defense for killing a sleeping partner?

Answer: No. Battered woman syndrome must be competently proved and does not automatically supply every element of self-defense; the governing law and facts must establish the statutory defense or a separate statutory exemption.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) and R.A. No. 9262, Section 26 govern traditional self-defense and the statutory battered-woman defense. People of the Philippines v. Marivic Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004, teaches that Battered woman syndrome must be proved through its elements and expert evidence; absent actual unlawful aggression at the killing, complete self-defense fails, though circumstances may mitigate.

Application: The partner's being asleep ordinarily negates present unlawful aggression under Article 11, but properly proved statutory BWS must be independently evaluated.

Conclusion: No automatic acquittal follows from a history of abuse alone.

Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) and R.A. No. 9262, Section 26 govern traditional self-defense and the statutory battered-woman defense. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Marivic Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004.
Traditional self-defense requires unlawful aggression, while Section 26 may apply to a victim-survivor found by the court to be suffering from battered woman syndrome under the statute.

G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004; ponente: Panganiban, J.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Self-defense indispensable element
What is the indispensable element of self-defense, and what follows if it is absent?

Answer: Unlawful aggression is indispensable; without actual or imminent unlawful aggression, complete or incomplete self-defense generally cannot be appreciated.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) requires unlawful aggression, reasonable necessity of the means, and lack of sufficient provocation. People of the Philippines v. Marivic Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004, teaches that Battered woman syndrome must be proved through its elements and expert evidence; absent actual unlawful aggression at the killing, complete self-defense fails, though circumstances may mitigate.

Application: Past threats unaccompanied by an actual or imminent attack at the time of the killing do not supply unlawful aggression.

Conclusion: Self-defense fails when unlawful aggression is absent, subject to another applicable defense or statute.

Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) requires unlawful aggression, reasonable necessity of the means, and lack of sufficient provocation. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Marivic Genosa, G.R. No. 135981, January 15, 2004.
The other requisites have nothing to prevent or repel without an unlawful attack.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Avoidance of greater evil
Enumerate the requisites of avoidance of a greater evil or injury.

Answer: The evil sought to be avoided must actually exist; the injury feared must be greater than that caused; and there must be no other practical and less harmful means of preventing it.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(4) states the justification. Sonia Ty v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 149275, September 27, 2004, teaches that Avoidance of a greater evil requires an actual and imminent evil, an injury feared greater than the injury caused, and no less harmful practical means.

Application: Issuing a worthless check merely to postpone business loss does not meet an actual imminent evil when lawful alternatives exist.

Conclusion: All three requisites must be proved for complete justification.
Revised Penal Code Article 11(4) states the justification. Case authority: Sonia Ty v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 149275, September 27, 2004.
The defense balances imminent harms and is construed from objective facts, not financial pressure or speculative fear.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Necessity and economic pressure
A business owner issues unfunded checks because suppliers threaten to stop deliveries and the enterprise may close; is avoidance of greater evil a defense to a penal statute?

Answer: No on those facts. Ordinary economic pressure is not the actual, imminent greater evil contemplated by Article 11(4), particularly when lawful alternatives exist.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(4) provides the defense; the special penal law's elements remain controlling. Sonia Ty v. People of the Philippines, G.R. Application: The owner could renegotiate, disclose the lack of funds, or cease purchases rather than issue prohibited checks.

Conclusion: The justification fails.
Revised Penal Code Article 11(4) provides the defense; the special penal law's elements remain controlling. Case authority: Sonia Ty v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 149275, September 27, 2004.
Necessity requires a concrete emergency and proportional choice of the least harmful means, not convenience or fear of commercial loss.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Obedience to superior order and good faith

A subordinate disbursing officer follows a facially lawful written presidential instruction, after ordinary verification, and has no notice of illegality; can good faith negate liability for intentional malversation?

Answer: Yes, when the charged mode requires criminal intent and the subordinate reasonably and honestly believed the order lawful; the exact elements and Article 11(6) must still be examined.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 3, 11(6), and 217 govern dolo, obedience to a lawful order issued for a lawful purpose, and malversation. Melchor Tabuena v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. Nos. 103501-03, February 17, 1997, teaches that Good-faith obedience to a lawful-appearing order of a superior may negate criminal intent when the subordinate had no reason to question it.

Application: A regular written instruction within apparent authority, checked through normal channels, differs from a manifestly illegal command.

Conclusion: Good faith may produce acquittal if it defeats the mens rea required by the charged mode.

Revised Penal Code Articles 3, 11(6), and 217 govern dolo, obedience to a lawful order issued for a lawful purpose, and malversation. Case authority: Melchor Tabuena v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. Nos. 103501-03, February 17, 1997.
Public officers are not automatically immune, but good faith may negate criminal intent where reliance is reasonable and no red flag demands inquiry.

May a subordinate invoke obedience to a superior who expressly orders destruction of public records to conceal a crime?

Answer: No. Article 11(6) justifies obedience only when the order is for a lawful purpose; a manifestly criminal command must not be obeyed.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(6) requires an order issued by a superior for a lawful purpose and lawful means of obedience. Melchor Tabuena v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. Application: Destroying records to conceal an offense is facially unlawful, so reliance on rank is unreasonable.

Conclusion: The subordinate remains liable according to participation and intent.

Revised Penal Code Article 11(6) requires an order issued by a superior for a lawful purpose and lawful means of obedience. Case authority: Melchor Tabuena v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. Nos. 103501-03, February 17, 1997.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Incomplete self-defense
When may incomplete self-defense mitigate criminal liability?

Answer: Unlawful aggression must be present. If a majority of the requisites of self-defense is proved but the justification is incomplete, Article 69 authorizes a privileged reduction by one or two degrees according to the number and nature of the conditions present; a lesser showing may be evaluated under Article 13(1).

L-33466-67, April 20, 1983, teaches that Unlawful aggression is indispensable to complete self-defense; where most but not all requisites exist, incomplete self-defense may mitigate liability.

Application: If the victim attacked first but the accused used clearly excessive force, incomplete self-defense may apply depending on the other proved requisites.

Conclusion: Liability remains, with mitigation determined under Articles 69 and 13(1).

Revised Penal Code Articles 11(1), 13(1), and 69 govern complete and incomplete justifying circumstances. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Glicerio Narvaez, G.R. Nos. L-33466-67, April 20, 1983.
Unlawful aggression remains indispensable; imperfection in reasonable necessity or lack of provocation may reduce rather than erase liability.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Reasonable necessity in self-defense
An aggressor slaps the accused once and retreats unarmed; the accused pursues and fatally stabs him. Was the means reasonably necessary?

Answer: No. The aggression had ceased, and pursuing with deadly force was neither necessary nor proportionate to prevent or repel it.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) requires reasonable necessity of the means employed and continuing unlawful aggression. People of the Philippines v. Glicerio Narvaez, G.R. Nos. Application: The retreat ended the immediate attack, while the accused initiated a new pursuit with lethal force.

Conclusion: Complete self-defense fails.

Revised Penal Code Article 11(1) requires reasonable necessity of the means employed and continuing unlawful aggression. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Glicerio Narvaez, G.R. Nos. L-33466-67, April 20, 1983.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Proximate cause
Define proximate cause in felony liability.

Answer: It is the cause which, in a natural and continuous sequence unbroken by an efficient intervening cause, produces the injury and without which the result would not have occurred.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 4(1) makes one committing an intentional felony liable for its natural and logical consequences. Alexander D. Urbano v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-72964, January 7, 1988, teaches that Felony liability requires that the accused's act be the proximate cause of the resulting harm without an efficient intervening cause.

Application: A wound directly producing fatal bleeding is proximate; a later wholly independent cause may break the chain.

Conclusion: Criminal liability for the result depends on proven legal causation.

Revised Penal Code Article 4(1) makes one committing an intentional felony liable for its natural and logical consequences. Case authority: Alexander D. Urbano v. Intermediate Appellate Court, G.R. No. L-72964, January 7, 1988.
The accused's act need not be the only cause, but the prosecution must prove the causal chain beyond reasonable doubt.

After a minor wound has completely healed, the victim dies months later from an independent disease medically unrelated to it; is the assailant liable for the death?

Application: Complete healing and an unrelated fatal disease sever the causal sequence on the stated medical proof.

Conclusion: Liability remains for the injury actually caused, not homicide.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Favorable retroactivity
A penal amendment enacted while an appeal is pending reduces the penalty for the offense; which penalty applies?

Answer: The more favorable amendatory law applies retroactively to the accused, unless the accused is a habitual criminal within the statutory exception or the new law provides otherwise consistently with the Constitution.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 22 gives favorable penal laws retroactive effect; Article III, Section 22 bars disadvantageous ex post facto laws. People of the Philippines v. Martin Simon, G.R. No. 93028, July 29, 1994, teaches that A penal amendment favorable to the accused applies retroactively, subject to the habitual-delinquent exception, and penalty rules must follow the amended statute.

Application: Because judgment is on appeal and the new range is lighter, the accused receives the benefit.

Conclusion: The amended favorable penalty controls.

Revised Penal Code Article 22 gives favorable penal laws retroactive effect; Article III, Section 22 bars disadvantageous ex post facto laws. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Martin Simon, G.R. No. 93028, July 29, 1994.
Finality is not required while the case remains pending, and courts apply the reduced penalty according to the amendment.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Midterm • Prospectivity of harsher penal law
Congress increases the penalty for an offense after the accused's completed act but before trial; may the higher penalty be imposed?

Answer: No. A harsher penal law applies prospectively, and retroactive use would violate both Article 22's favorable-retroactivity framework and the ex post facto prohibition.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 22 and Constitution Article III, Section 22 govern temporal application. People of the Philippines v. Martin Simon, G.R. No. 93028, July 29, 1994, teaches that A penal amendment favorable to the accused applies retroactively, subject to the habitual-delinquent exception, and penalty rules must follow the amended statute.

Application: The increase occurred after the conduct and would aggravate punishment retroactively.

Conclusion: Only the earlier penalty may be imposed.
Revised Penal Code Article 22 and Constitution Article III, Section 22 govern temporal application. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Martin Simon, G.R. No. 93028, July 29, 1994.
An offender is judged under the law at the time of the act unless a later law is more favorable and legally applicable.

Enumerate the requisites of treachery as a qualifying or generic aggravating circumstance.

May homicide and robbery committed solely in furtherance of rebellion be separately complexed with rebellion under Article 48?

Answer: No. Under the political-offense doctrine, common crimes shown to be necessary or in furtherance of rebellion are absorbed in rebellion rather than complexed under Article 48.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 48 and 134, as construed in the controlling rebellion doctrine, govern. People of the Philippines v. Amado V. Hernandez, G.R. No. L-6025, May 30, 1964, teaches that Common crimes committed in furtherance of rebellion are absorbed and are not complexed with rebellion under Article 48.

Application: If the prosecution proves the acts were committed only to advance the uprising, they are absorbed.

Conclusion: The charge is simple rebellion, without prejudice to proof of independently motivated crimes.
Revised Penal Code Articles 48 and 134, as construed in the controlling rebellion doctrine, govern. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Amado V. Hernandez, G.R. No. L-6025, May 30, 1964.

A rebel member uses the uprising as cover to kill a personal creditor for private revenge; is the killing absorbed in rebellion?

Answer: No. A common crime motivated by a private purpose and not committed in furtherance of the political uprising retains independent criminal character.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 134 and 48, under the political-offense doctrine, distinguish rebellion acts from private crimes. People of the Philippines v. Amado V. Hernandez, G.R. No. L-6025, May 30, 1964, teaches that Common crimes committed in furtherance of rebellion are absorbed and are not complexed with rebellion under Article 48.

Application: Killing a creditor to erase a personal debt advances no rebel objective and rests on a private motive.

Conclusion: The homicide or murder may be separately prosecuted.

Revised Penal Code Articles 134 and 48, under the political-offense doctrine, distinguish rebellion acts from private crimes. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Amado V. Hernandez, G.R. No. L-6025, May 30, 1964.
Membership in a rebellion does not immunize all conduct during the uprising.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Aberratio ictus
Define aberratio ictus and state its usual effect on criminal liability.

Answer: Aberratio ictus is a mistake in the blow: the offender directs an attack at the intended victim but strikes another; intent generally transfers, with Article 48 or other penalty rules governing the resulting offenses.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 4(1), 48, and 49 address consequences, complex crimes, and differing intended and committed offenses. People of the Philippines v. Julio Guillen, G.R. No. L-1477, January 18, 1950, teaches that Aberratio ictus does not erase intent; a single act causing the intended and unintended grave felonies may produce a complex crime under Article 48.

Application: A bomb thrown at A that instead kills B leaves the thrower liable for B's death and any separate attempted offense against A as legally complexed or treated.

Conclusion: Liability follows the natural felonious consequences subject to the proper penalty rule.

Revised Penal Code Articles 4(1), 48, and 49 address consequences, complex crimes, and differing intended and committed offenses. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Julio Guillen, G.R. No. L-1477, January 18, 1950.
The error does not erase dolo because the actor intended a felonious attack.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Single act causing intended and unintended felonies
An attacker throws one grenade at a public official intending to kill him; the official survives but a bystander dies. Is the bystander's death accidental in the exculpatory sense?

Answer: No. The offender intentionally committed a felony and is liable for the natural consequences, including the unintended victim's death; the proper complex-crime and penalty rules apply.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 4(1), 48, and 49 govern transferred intent and multiple results. People of the Philippines v. Julio Guillen, G.R. Application: The single unlawful act caused both the attempted intended killing and consummated death.

Conclusion: The offender is criminally liable for the resulting complex or legally appropriate crimes.
Revised Penal Code Articles 4(1), 48, and 49 govern transferred intent and multiple results. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Julio Guillen, G.R. No. L-1477, January 18, 1950.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Conspiracy by coordinated acts
Can conspiracy be proved without a written agreement or eyewitness to the planning meeting?

Answer: Yes. Conspiracy may be inferred from coordinated acts before, during, and after the offense that unmistakably reveal a common design, though proof must be beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 8 defines conspiracy; Article 17 governs principals. Dandy L. Dungo v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015, teaches that Presence and coordinated acts during hazing may establish participation and conspiracy under the then-governing Anti-Hazing Law when proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Application: Blocking the victim's escape while another executes the planned attack and jointly fleeing under prior coordination can evidence conspiracy.

Conclusion: Once conspiracy is proved, each conspirator is liable for acts in furtherance of the common design.
Revised Penal Code Article 8 defines conspiracy; Article 17 governs principals. Case authority: Dandy L. Dungo v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015.

Is presence at the scene of a group crime, without more, enough to make a bystander a conspirator?

Answer: No. Conspiracy requires intentional agreement and participation in the common design; mere presence or passive knowledge is not enough, unless a special statute creates a distinct presumption or offense.

Application: A person who watches from a lawful location, does not aid, and leaves independently is not made a conspirator by proximity alone.

Conclusion: No conspiratorial liability attaches without proof of agreement and participation.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Mala prohibita and statutory intent
Distinguish mala in se from mala prohibita offenses.

Answer: Mala in se are inherently wrongful and ordinarily require criminal intent; mala prohibita are not inherently immoral but are prohibited by positive law for public-policy reasons, so voluntary commission of the prohibited act may suffice unless the enactment requires a particular mental state.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 3 governs felonies, while the text, purpose, and inherent nature of the act determine each penal offense's elements. Dandy L. Dungo v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015, teaches that Mala in se are inherently immoral acts for which criminal intent generally governs, while mala prohibita are acts made wrongful by positive law for public-policy reasons; the penal enactment's text and the act's inherent nature, not the code-or-special-law label alone, control.

Application: Homicide is malum in se, while technical malversation under the Code is commonly treated as malum prohibitum; some special-law offenses may nevertheless be mala in se.

Conclusion: The act's inherent character and governing enactment—not the code-versus-special-law label alone—control.

Revised Penal Code Article 3 governs felonies, while the text, purpose, and inherent nature of the act determine each penal offense's elements. Case authority: Dandy L. Dungo v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015.
The location of an offense in the Revised Penal Code or a special law is not conclusive; the prosecution must still prove every statutory element, voluntariness, and any express mental state.

G.R. No. 209464, July 1, 2015; ponente: Mendoza, J.

Criminal Law I
LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Separate statutory offenses from one conduct
The same unlawful discharge violates the Mining Act, Clean Water Act, and environmental decree, each requiring a different element; does one prosecution automatically bar the others?

Answer: No. Separate prosecutions may proceed when each statute defines a distinct offense requiring proof of an element the others do not, subject to double-jeopardy and legislative-intent limits.

Legal Basis: Constitution Article III, Section 21 and the elements of the applicable special laws govern; Revised Penal Code Book One applies only as made suppletory. Nelson Loney v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 152644, February 10, 2006, teaches that Distinct statutory offenses arising from the same acts may be separately prosecuted when each law requires proof of an element the others do not.

Application: If one law requires operating without a permit, another pollution beyond standards, and another prohibited disposal, none is necessarily identical.

Conclusion: The prosecutions are not automatically duplicative.

Constitution Article III, Section 21 and the elements of the applicable special laws govern; Revised Penal Code Book One applies only as made suppletory. Case authority: Nelson Loney v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 152644, February 10, 2006.
The same physical conduct can produce distinct legal offenses when Congress protects different interests through different elements.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Conspiracy and individual participation
Three accused agree to assault V; one unexpectedly steals V's phone for a purely personal purpose after the assault. Are all conspirators liable for theft?

Answer: No. Conspirators are liable for acts in furtherance of the common design and natural consequences, not an independent act outside the agreement done for a purely personal purpose.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 8 and 17 define conspiracy and principals. People of the Philippines v. Quijada, G.R. Application: The agreed object was assault, and the unplanned personal theft neither advanced nor naturally implemented it.

Conclusion: Only the thief is liable for the independent theft absent proof the others adopted it.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Death pending appeal
What happens when an accused dies while a criminal conviction is still on appeal?

Answer: Death pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability based solely on the offense, because the conviction has not become final; independent civil liability from another source may still be pursued against the estate.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 89(1), Civil Code Articles 19, 20, 21, and 2176, and Rule 111 govern extinction and independent civil actions. People of the Philippines v. Rogelio Bayotas, G.R. No. 102007, September 2, 1994, teaches that Death of the accused pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto, without prejudice to an independent civil action based on another source of obligation.

Application: If the only damages award is ex delicto, it is extinguished; a separately supportable contract or tort claim may be filed in the proper civil proceeding.

Conclusion: The criminal case and civil liability ex delicto are dismissed.

Revised Penal Code Article 89(1), Civil Code Articles 19, 20, 21, and 2176, and Rule 111 govern extinction and independent civil actions. Case authority: People of the Philippines v. Rogelio Bayotas, G.R. No. 102007, September 2, 1994.
The appeal opens the entire judgment, so death prevents final criminal adjudication.

Conclusion: Execution of the ex delicto award is unavailable.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Effect of absolute pardon
Does an absolute pardon erase the fact of conviction and automatically restore the pardoned person's former public office?

Answer: No. Pardon remits penalties and disabilities within its terms but does not rewrite history, declare innocence, or automatically reinstate a forfeited office.

Legal Basis: Constitution Article VII, Section 19 and Revised Penal Code Article 36 govern pardon and accessory penalties. Cristeta A. Monsanto v. Deputy Executive Secretary Fulgencio Factoran, Jr., G.R. No. 78239, February 9, 1989, teaches that Absolute pardon removes penalties and disabilities but does not erase the historical fact of conviction or automatically restore a forfeited public office.

Application: A former officer may regain eligibility if the pardon so provides, but cannot demand automatic return and back salary as though no conviction occurred.

Conclusion: The conviction remains a historical fact and office is not automatically restored.

Constitution Article VII, Section 19 and Revised Penal Code Article 36 govern pardon and accessory penalties. Case authority: Cristeta A. Monsanto v. Deputy Executive Secretary Fulgencio Factoran, Jr., G.R. No. 78239, February 9, 1989.

Distinguish pardon from amnesty.

Application: A convicted individual may receive pardon, while participants in a defined uprising may invoke a duly proclaimed and concurred-in amnesty.

Conclusion: Their sources, beneficiaries, timing, and legal effects differ.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Reckless imprudence as a quasi-offense
Is reckless imprudence merely a way of committing each resulting felony, or is it a distinct quasi-offense?

Answer: It is a distinct quasi-offense under Article 365 that punishes the negligent mental attitude, with all consequences alleged in one Information and considered under Article 365's penalty scheme; Article 48 does not complex those consequences.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Articles 3 and 365 govern culpa and criminal negligence. Francis O. Morales v. People of the Philippines, G.R. Application: A single careless collision causing death, injuries, and property damage must be prosecuted in one reckless-imprudence Information accounting for every consequence.

Conclusion: Liability is for the Article 365 quasi-offense and its proven consequences.
Revised Penal Code Articles 3 and 365 govern culpa and criminal negligence. Case authority: Francis O. Morales v. People of the Philippines, G.R. No. 240337, January 4, 2022.

May a convicted accused pursue an ordinary appeal and simultaneously apply for probation?

When may passion or obfuscation mitigate criminal liability?

Answer: It may mitigate when a lawful and sufficient stimulus naturally produces powerful emotion that precedes the crime closely enough to dominate reason, and it is not based on revenge or an unlawful sentiment.

Application: An immediate violent reaction to witnessing a grave wrong against a close relative may qualify; returning armed after hours of calm planning generally does not.

Conclusion: The mitigating circumstance applies only when its causal and temporal requirements are proved.

When is a person who did not physically execute the crime liable as a principal by inducement?

Answer: The inducement must be made directly with the intention of procuring the crime and must be the determining cause that moves the executor to commit it.

Legal Basis: Revised Penal Code Article 17(2), read with Article 8 where conspiracy is alleged, governs principals by inducement. People of the Philippines v. Florenda Manzanilla y De Asis, G.R. Application: If a dominant organizer promises payment expressly conditioned on killing V and the killer acts because of that promise, inducement is principal participation.

Conclusion: Liability as principal by inducement requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of both intent and decisive causation.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD401 • Final • Accomplice distinguished from conspirator
Distinguish an accomplice from a conspirator who is liable as a principal.

Answer: A conspirator agrees to and adopts the criminal design, making acts in furtherance attributable to all; an accomplice knows the design only after its formation and knowingly cooperates through previous or simultaneous acts that are not indispensable.

Application: A lookout who joined the plan beforehand may be a principal-conspirator; one later asked to provide nonessential transport with full knowledge may be an accomplice.

Conclusion: The prosecution must prove the level of participation rather than presume collective principal liability.

After an information is filed, the Secretary of Justice reverses the prosecutor and directs dismissal; must the trial judge automatically dismiss the case?

Answer: No. The prosecutor may move to dismiss, but the court must independently evaluate and grant or deny the motion because the case is already under judicial control.

Legal Basis: Rule 110, Section 5 of the Rules of Court. Once an information is filed, disposition of the criminal case belongs to the court; the prosecutor may move to dismiss after review, but cannot impose that view on the judge, who must independently grant or deny the motion.

Application: The executive review is persuasive to the prosecutor but cannot displace the judge's duty to decide the pending motion from the record and law.

Conclusion: Dismissal is not automatic.
Rule 110, Section 5 of the Rules of Court. G.R. No. L-53373, June 30, 1987, Gancayco, J. — petition dismissed for lack of merit
Once an information is filed, the court controls its disposition although prosecution remains under the public prosecutor's direction.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Quiz • prejudicial question
A bigamy accused asks to suspend the criminal case because a later-filed civil action seeks to annul the first marriage for fraud; is there necessarily a prejudicial question?

Answer: No. A prejudicial question requires a previously instituted civil action whose resolution is logically antecedent and determinative of criminal liability, and annulment for a voidable defect does not retroactively erase a marriage that existed when the second marriage was contracted.

Legal Basis: Rule 111, Sections 6 and 7 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: The civil case was later filed and its requested annulment would not necessarily negate an element existing at the time of the alleged bigamy.

Conclusion: The criminal case should not be suspended on these facts.

When is an accused entitled to preliminary investigation under the Rules of Court?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • judicial probable cause for arrest warrant
May an RTC judge issue an arrest warrant merely by adopting the prosecutor's certification without examining the supporting record?

Answer: No. The judge must personally evaluate the prosecutor's resolution and supporting evidence and may require additional evidence when doubtful; personal examination of witnesses is not invariably required, but personal determination is.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution and Rule 112, Section 5 of the Rules of Court. A judge must personally determine probable cause from adequate supporting evidence before issuing an arrest warrant; a bare, materially unreliable accusation cannot justify loss of liberty.

Application: A bare adoption reveals no independent evaluation of whether facts support a well-founded belief that the accused committed the offense.

Conclusion: The warrant is defective absent personal judicial determination.

Judicial probable cause is a nondelegable personal determination based on the record, not a rubber stamp of prosecutorial probable cause.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • in-flagrante warrantless arrest
Police receive a tip describing a drug courier, stop the identified passenger, empty his pockets, find drugs, and only then arrest him; is the arrest valid in flagrante delicto?

Answer: No. An in-flagrante arrest requires an overt act indicating that the person is committing, has committed, or is attempting an offense in the officer's presence; a tip and a search cannot manufacture that overt act.

Legal Basis: Rule 113, Section 5(a) and Rule 126, Section 13 of the Rules of Court; Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) of the Constitution. An anonymous tip without an observed overt act does not establish an in-flagrante or hot-pursuit arrest; a search incident cannot precede and create the justification for arrest, and evidence from the unlawful search is excluded.

Application: The officers observed no criminal conduct before the intrusive search, so neither the arrest nor a search incident to it is valid.

Conclusion: The drugs are inadmissible and the arrest unlawful.

A lawful arrest must precede a search incident; an unverified tip alone does not satisfy the overt-act requirement.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • hot-pursuit warrantless arrest
Within an hour of a stabbing, officers arrive, see the bleeding victim, receive the victim's immediate identification of a nearby suspect, and arrest that suspect; is hot-pursuit arrest available?

Answer: Yes, if the total circumstances give the officers probable cause based on personal knowledge that the offense has just been committed and the suspect committed it.

Legal Basis: Rule 113, Section 5(b) of the Rules of Court. A hot-pursuit arrest requires that an offense has just been committed and that the arresting officer has probable cause based on personal knowledge of facts or circumstances indicating that the person arrested committed it; facts promptly relayed and verified at the scene may satisfy that standard.

Conclusion: The warrantless hot-pursuit arrest is valid.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • arrest of escaped prisoner
May a convicted prisoner who escapes while being transferred be arrested without a warrant days later?

Answer: Yes. An escaped prisoner may be arrested without a warrant at any time and place in the Philippines.

Legal Basis: Rule 113, Sections 5(c) and 13 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: The escape places the prisoner within the express warrantless-arrest category; delay does not restore a warrant requirement.

Conclusion: The recapture is valid without a warrant.

A shopkeeper personally sees a customer conceal merchandise and pass the exit without paying; may the shopkeeper arrest the customer without a warrant?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • search incident to lawful arrest
Officers unlawfully search a pedestrian, discover contraband, and then announce an arrest based on the contraband; may the evidence be justified as a search incident to arrest?

Answer: No. A search incident is valid only after or substantially contemporaneous with a lawful arrest supported by grounds independent of the search.

Legal Basis: Rule 126, Section 13 of the Rules of Court and Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) of the Constitution. An anonymous tip without an observed overt act does not establish an in-flagrante or hot-pursuit arrest; a search incident cannot precede and create the justification for arrest, and evidence from the unlawful search is excluded.

Application: The officers had no lawful arrest basis before opening the pedestrian's belongings; the contraband is fruit of the unconstitutional search.

Conclusion: The evidence must be excluded.

Rule 126, Section 13 of the Rules of Court and Article III, Sections 2 and 3(2) of the Constitution. G.R. No. 200370, June 7, 2017, Leonen, J. — conviction reversed; petitioner acquitted and ordered released
A search incident cannot precede and supply the probable cause for the arrest it supposedly accompanies.
Mario Veridiano y Sapi v. People of the Philippines

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • requisites of a search warrant
Enumerate the constitutional and procedural requisites for issuance of a search warrant?

Answer: There must be probable cause connected with one specific offense, personally determined by a judge after searching examination under oath of the complainant and witnesses, and the warrant must particularly describe the place and things to be seized.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution and Rule 126, Sections 3 to 6 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: Each requirement limits exploratory searches and ensures the judge, not police, decides probable cause.

Conclusion: Failure of a material requisite invalidates the warrant.

A search warrant requires judicial probable cause, oath, particularity, and relation to one specific offense.

A single warrant authorizes seizure of evidence of tax fraud, estafa, and falsification based on one omnibus application; is the warrant valid?

Legal Basis: Rule 126, Section 4 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: The application aggregates separate offenses without limiting the officers to evidence of one defined violation.

Conclusion: The warrant is void for violating the one-specific-offense rule.

A warrant authorizes officers to search an entire twelve-unit building for 'documents and things connected with illegal activity' without identifying a unit or item; is it sufficiently particular?

Application: The building-wide and generic description exposes unrelated occupants and property to an exploratory rummage.

Conclusion: The warrant is a prohibited general warrant.

While lawfully serving a warrant for an unlicensed firearm in a living room, an officer sees on an open table a transparent sachet whose incriminating nature is immediately apparent; may it be seized?

At midnight, an officer sees a man repeatedly peering into closed stores and gripping a gun-shaped bulge at his waist; may the officer conduct a limited pat-down?

Application: The repeated casing behavior, time, location, and weapon-shaped bulge create reasonable suspicion; the frisk must remain confined to discovering weapons.

Conclusion: A limited protective pat-down is reasonable.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • checkpoint searches
At a routine checkpoint with no individualized suspicion, may officers compel every motorist to open locked luggage for a full search?

Answer: No. A routine checkpoint generally permits a brief visual inspection; an extensive search requires consent, probable cause, or another recognized exception.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution and Rule 126 of the Rules of Court. An anonymous tip without an observed overt act does not establish an in-flagrante or hot-pursuit arrest; a search incident cannot precede and create the justification for arrest, and evidence from the unlawful search is excluded.

Application: Opening locked luggage is substantially more intrusive than visual inspection, and no overt act or particular fact supports probable cause.

Conclusion: The compelled full search is unreasonable.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • bail as a matter of right
When is bail a matter of right before conviction?

Answer: Bail is a matter of right before or after conviction by a first-level court, and before RTC conviction for an offense not punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 13 of the Constitution and Rule 114, Section 4 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: An RTC accused facing a maximum penalty below reclusion perpetua is entitled to reasonable bail before conviction.

Conclusion: The judge must admit the accused to bail upon sufficient security or authorized recognizance.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • bail pending appeal after RTC conviction
An RTC convicts an accused of an offense carrying twelve years' imprisonment, and none of Rule 114's listed risk factors is proven; is bail pending appeal automatic?

Answer: No. After RTC conviction, bail is discretionary; absence of the listed circumstances preserves discretion but does not create a right to release.

Legal Basis: Rule 114, Section 5 of the Rules of Court. After RTC conviction, bail pending appeal is discretionary and must be granted only for strong reasons with grave caution; absence of the enumerated bail-negating circumstances does not make release automatic.

Application: The conviction ends the presumption-based entitlement, so the applicant must show strong reasons while the court weighs flight, recidivism, public safety, and the case circumstances.

Conclusion: The court may still deny bail through a reasoned exercise of discretion.

The prosecution objects to bail for an offense punishable by reclusion perpetua, and the judge denies bail solely from the information without a hearing; is the order proper?

Application: The information proves only the accusation, not the strength of evidence; the accused must be allowed to test the prosecution's showing.

Conclusion: The summary denial should be set aside for a proper bail hearing.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Midterm • evidence of guilt strong
At a murder bail hearing, may the judge finally determine guilt beyond reasonable doubt?

Answer: No. The inquiry is limited to whether the prosecution evidence of guilt is strong; it is provisional and does not preclude a different judgment after full trial.

Legal Basis: Rule 114, Sections 7 and 8 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: The judge should assess weight for bail without converting the hearing into the merits trial or prejudging defenses not yet fully presented.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • arraignment essentials
What acts are indispensable to a valid arraignment under the current in-person and videoconferencing rules?

Answer: The accused must personally participate, receive a copy of the complaint or information, have it read in a language or dialect known to the accused unless validly waived, and personally enter a plea. The proceeding may be in person or by court-authorized videoconferencing, which is now the preferred mode for arraignment unless the court directs otherwise.

Legal Basis: Rule 116, Section 1 of the Rules of Court and Sections 1(d), 4, and 35 of A.M. No. 24-11-02-SC, effective February 16, 2026. Videoconferencing is the preferred mode for arraignment unless the court deems in-person appearance appropriate; remote participation satisfies the accused's right to be present, but the accused must still personally enter the plea and all Rule 116 safeguards remain applicable.

Application: Counsel cannot enter the plea for an absent accused. If arraignment is remote, real-time personal participation and the clerk's certification preserve the Rule 116 safeguards.

Conclusion: A valid arraignment requires the accused's personal, informed plea, whether the authorized courtroom is physical or remote.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • arraignment, counsel, and due process
A judge treats a bail hearing as trial, receives affidavits not formally offered, denies cross-examination, and convicts without allowing defense evidence; is the judgment valid?

Answer: No. Even with a plea on record, criminal conviction requires the ordered trial process, counsel, confrontation, formal offer of evidence, and a meaningful opportunity to defend.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 14 of the Constitution and Rules 115, 116, and 119 of the Rules of Court. A conviction cannot rest on an improvised proceeding that denied the accused the ordered stages of trial, confrontation, cross-examination, presentation of a defense, and consideration only of formally offered evidence.

Application: The improvised proceeding eliminated core adversarial safeguards and relied on material never tested or formally offered.

Conclusion: The conviction is void for denial of due process.

May an accused demand acceptance of a plea to a lesser offense over the prosecutor's and offended party's objections?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • guilty plea to capital offense
An accused pleads guilty to a capital offense and the prosecution presents no witness despite repeated opportunities; may the court convict on the plea alone?

Answer: No. The court must conduct a searching inquiry, require proof of guilt and precise culpability, and allow defense evidence; the plea alone cannot sustain conviction.

Legal Basis: Rule 116, Section 3 of the Rules of Court. For a plea of guilty to a capital offense, the trial judge must conduct a searching inquiry, require prosecution proof of guilt and precise culpability, and allow defense evidence; Pagal applied the mandatory safeguards and, after the prosecution repeatedly failed to prove guilt, acquitted.

Application: The prosecution's failure to prove the charge leaves the constitutional burden unsatisfied notwithstanding the plea.

Conclusion: Conviction cannot rest solely on the improvident plea.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • double jeopardy requisites
Enumerate the requisites of double jeopardy and apply them to a dismissal before arraignment?

Answer: There must be a valid complaint or information, a court of competent jurisdiction, arraignment and valid plea, and conviction, acquittal, or dismissal without the accused's express consent; a pre-arraignment dismissal generally lacks prior jeopardy.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 21 of the Constitution and Rule 117, Section 7 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: Because no plea was entered, one indispensable attachment point is absent even if the same charge is later refiled.

Conclusion: The pre-arraignment dismissal ordinarily does not bar reprosecution on double-jeopardy grounds.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • provisional dismissal
A serious offense is provisionally dismissed while the accused remains silent and the victim receives no prior notice; does the two-year Rule 117 bar automatically make dismissal permanent?

Answer: No. The time bar requires the accused's express, unequivocal consent and notice to the offended party, with service of the dismissal order on the public prosecutor; silence does not satisfy express consent.

Legal Basis: Rule 117, Section 8 of the Rules of Court. Conclusion: The State is not automatically barred by the Rule 117 time bar.

After valid arraignment and notice of trial, an accused deliberately absconds without justification; may trial continue in the accused's absence?

Conclusion: Trial in absentia is permissible.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • discharge of an accused as state witness
May the court discharge a co-accused as a state witness when equally strong direct evidence is available from an uncharged eyewitness?

Answer: Ordinarily no. Discharge requires absolute necessity for the testimony, no other direct evidence available for proper prosecution, substantial corroboration, absence of being the most guilty, and no prior conviction for an offense involving moral turpitude.

Legal Basis: Rule 119, Sections 17 and 18 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: The available uncharged eyewitness defeats absolute necessity and the absence-of-other-direct-evidence requisites.

Conclusion: The discharge motion should be denied.

An accused files a demurrer without prior leave and the court denies it; what procedural consequence follows?

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • speedy trial and excluded delay
Does every postponement beyond a stated trial period automatically require dismissal for violation of speedy trial?

Answer: No. The court must account for periods expressly excluded by Rule 119 and R.A. No. 8493, the reasons and attribution for delay, assertion of the right, and resulting prejudice; only unjustified violation warrants the prescribed remedy.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 14(2) of the Constitution; Rule 119, Sections 1 to 9; and Republic Act No. 8493. Speedy-disposition analysis begins with formal complaint and preliminary investigation, excludes justified periods, considers complexity, reasons, assertion and prejudice, and requires timely invocation; the contrary fact-finding reckoning rule was abandoned.

Application: Delay caused by a defense-requested competency examination or a genuinely unavailable essential witness may be excluded rather than charged to the State.

Conclusion: The court must compute and balance the delay, not dismiss mechanically.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • speedy disposition of cases

An accused waits silently through a complex preliminary investigation, invokes speedy disposition only after information is filed, and counts a prior fact-finding audit in the delay; is dismissal automatic?

Answer: No. Cagang reckons from the formal complaint and preliminary investigation, examines complexity and justified periods, requires timely assertion, and treats acquiescence as possible waiver.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution and Rule 112 of the Rules of Court. Speedy-disposition analysis begins with formal complaint and preliminary investigation, excludes justified periods, considers complexity, reasons, assertion and prejudice, and requires timely invocation; the contrary fact-finding reckoning rule was abandoned.

Application: The fact-finding audit is excluded, complexity may justify time, and the accused's belated assertion weighs heavily against dismissal absent proven malice or actual prejudice.

Conclusion: The court must conduct the full Cagang analysis rather than dismiss by calendar alone.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • variance and necessarily included offense
An information alleges murder with treachery, but trial proves an unlawful killing without any qualifying circumstance; may the accused be convicted of homicide?

Answer: Yes. An accused may be convicted of an offense necessarily included in the offense charged when the allegations and proof establish the included offense beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Rule 120, Sections 4 and 5 of the Rules of Court. The Supreme Court promulgated the controlling rules on prosecution, preliminary investigation, arrest, bail, arraignment, trial, judgment, and post-judgment remedies in criminal cases.

Application: Homicide's elements are contained in murder; failure to prove treachery removes the qualification but not the proven unlawful killing.

Conclusion: Conviction for the included offense of homicide is permissible.

LEB Model Year 1 • Term 1 • JD601 • Final • finality of acquittal and Rule 65
The prosecution believes the trial court gravely misread evidence and seeks certiorari to reverse an acquittal, but it was fully heard and alleges no jurisdictional defect; may Rule 65 be used?

Answer: No. Reassessment of evidence is an appeal in disguise and is barred by finality of acquittal and double jeopardy; Rule 65 lies only against a void judgment produced by genuine grave abuse amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, including denial of the State's due process.

Legal Basis: Article III, Section 21 of the Constitution and Rule 65 in relation to Rule 120 of the Rules of Court. An acquittal is immediately final; the State may use Rule 65 only to show a void judgment caused by grave abuse or denial of its due process, not to obtain a forbidden review of evidentiary errors.

Application: The prosecution had a fair opportunity to litigate and merely disputes evidentiary conclusions, so no jurisdictional exception exists.

Conclusion: The certiorari petition must be dismissed.
